title: ACT Reading — Practice Test 2
summary: A full timed enhanced-ACT Reading section: 4 original passages, 36 questions, 40 minutes, with an explanation for every answer.

blocks.text: This is a complete practice **ACT Reading** section in the enhanced ACT format: **40 minutes** for **4 passages with 9 questions each (36 questions)**. The passages are a literary narrative (memoir), a pair of natural science passages, a humanities passage, and a social science passage with a small table. In the real test, 27 of the 36 questions are scored and one passage is unscored; you will not know which one. **Here all 36 questions count**, so treat every passage seriously. All passages and questions are original.

items: Sit somewhere quiet with no phone and no dictionary. Keep scrap paper for your passage map.
Start the timer and do not pause it. Aim for about **10 minutes per passage** (read for about 3–4 minutes, then answer).
There is no penalty for wrong answers on the ACT, so **answer every question**, even if you have to guess when time is short.
If a passage is taking too long, guess on the hardest question, mark it, and move on. Come back only if time is left.
Your result here is a **practice percentage**, not an official ACT scaled score (1–36).

questions.p:
Passage I — Literary Narrative: This passage is adapted from a memoir. The narrator remembers a summer she spent in her uncle's radio-repair shop in Tanta.

[1] I was sixteen when my grandmother's radio died, and since I had been the last person to touch it, I felt it was my job to fix it. My mother suggested that I take it to her brother, my uncle Sayed, who repaired radios in Tanta. So on the first Friday of the summer holiday, I carried it on the train from Cairo, wrapped in a bath towel like a sick cat, and arrived at his shop with a speech prepared.

[2] The shop was narrower than our kitchen at home. Shelves climbed all four walls, and on them sat radios of every age: wooden cabinets with cloth fronts, plastic transistor sets the color of old teeth. Each wore a paper tag on which my uncle had written a name and a single word: "hum," "silent," "crackles," "fades." It looked less like a workshop than a hospital ward, and the patients, I would soon learn, were treated in strict order of arrival, no matter how important their owners believed themselves to be.

[3] My uncle listened to my speech, unwrapped the radio, and placed it on the highest shelf, at the end of the line. "Your grandmother's turn will come," he said. "In the meantime, you can learn." I was offended. I had come to have something fixed, not to become an apprentice, and I said so. He only took down a different radio, one whose tag said "silent," set it in front of me, and asked me what was wrong with it. I turned it over, shook it, and at last admitted that I had no idea. "Good," he said. "Now you are ready to start listening."

[4] It took me most of the month to understand what he meant. Before he opened any set, he would switch it on and sit with his eyes half closed, turning the dial very slowly. A low, steady hum told him one thing; a crackle that grew worse when he tapped the case told him another. He said that a radio describes its own illness to anyone patient enough to hear it, and that most repairmen fail not because their hands are clumsy but because they are in a hurry to begin. I had always assumed that skill meant speed. Watching him, I began to suspect that it meant something closer to the opposite.

[5] In the weeks that followed, he taught me to use the soldering iron on a dead circuit board he kept for practice. My first joints were ugly gray lumps, and he made me melt each away and start again. He never once told me that a joint was good. Instead, one morning, he simply stopped checking them, and I realized, with a pride I have rarely felt since, that he had begun to trust my hands.

[6] The radio that changed things for me belonged to Umm Saber, a widow who lived above the bakery across the street. The heavy wooden set had been her husband's, and it had fallen silent in the spring. She came in almost every day to ask about it, never impatient, only hopeful, and each time my uncle told her, "Soon." One afternoon he set it on the bench in front of me and went out to buy tea. I understood that this was a test, and I was terrified of it.

[7] I did what he had taught me. I switched the set on and listened. There was no hum at all, which meant, I hoped, that the power was not even reaching the circuits. I opened the back, traced the wire from the plug, and found the fault almost at once: a connection near the switch had cracked loose. It took me ten minutes to repair and nearly an hour to believe that I had repaired it correctly. When my uncle returned, I had the radio playing an old song from a Cairo station, softly, so that it would not seem like boasting.

[8] He listened for a moment and then said, "You will take it to her." Umm Saber opened her door above the bakery, saw what I was holding, and pressed her hand to her mouth. Without a word, she set the radio on a small table by the window, exactly where, I could tell from a clean square in the dust, it had always stood, and she switched it on herself.

[9] My grandmother's radio was repaired on my last day in Tanta, by me, while my uncle pretended not to watch. I am an engineer now, and the systems I work on are far more complicated than anything on his shelves. But when something fails and my colleagues rush to replace parts, I still find myself sitting quietly for a minute first, listening, while someone asks me what I am waiting for.
questions.q: The passage is best described as the narrator's account of:
c: a quarrel with her uncle that she later regretted and tried to make up for.
a summer in which she learned a patient way of solving problems that she still uses.
the slow disappearance of the radio-repair trade in a provincial city.
a contest between herself and her uncle to see who could repair a neighbor's radio first.
questions.e: The passage moves from her arrival, through her uncle's lessons about listening, to her first real repair, and ends with her still 'listening' as an engineer. A is wrong: her irritation in paragraph 3 is brief and never becomes a quarrel; D is wrong because her uncle hands her the repair as a test, not a contest.

let the narrator attempt the repair on her own.

Passage II — Natural Science (Paired Passages): Passage A is adapted from an essay by a marine biologist; Passage B is adapted from a lecture by an oceanographer. Both scientists are fictional.

**PASSAGE A** (by Leila Haddad)

[1] When corals are exposed to water that is too warm for too long, they expel the tiny algae that live inside their tissues and supply most of their food. Without the algae, the coral's white skeleton shows through its clear tissue, and the reef appears to bleach. Bleaching is not instant death, but a coral that stays bleached for weeks may starve. For years, each new bleaching event has been reported as another step toward the end of reefs. That view, though understandable, leaves out something important: corals are not fixed objects. They are living communities, and living communities respond to pressure.

[2] Consider the evidence from reefs that already live in unusually warm water. In some shallow lagoons and enclosed seas, corals regularly survive summer temperatures that would bleach the same species elsewhere. My colleagues and I have moved fragments of such corals to cooler aquariums and then heated them again; many remain tolerant months later. This suggests that their tolerance is not only a temporary reaction but, at least partly, something the corals carry with them. Some of it may even be passed on: in a few studies, the young of tolerant parents have coped with heat better than other young corals.

[3] Corals also have more than one way to adjust. Some can exchange the algae they host for types that cope better with heat. Others appear to "remember" a mild heat stress, so that a second, stronger stress the following year does less damage. And because a single spawning event releases enormous numbers of larvae, the few individuals that happen to be most heat tolerant can, in principle, seed the next generation.

[4] None of this means that reefs are safe. It means that the future of reefs is not already written. If we reduce local harms such as pollution and overfishing, we give these natural responses room to work, and we may be able to help them along by raising tolerant corals in nurseries and planting them on damaged reefs. Abandoning reefs as lost causes would be a mistake precisely when they are showing us how they might survive.

**PASSAGE B** (by Tomas Lindqvist)

[1] No one who studies reefs doubts that corals can adjust to heat to some degree. The question that matters is not whether they can adapt but whether they can adapt fast enough. On that question, I am far less hopeful than many of my colleagues. Optimism is pleasant, but it should follow the evidence, not lead it.

[2] Adaptation through natural selection works across generations, and many reef-building corals take several years to reach the age at which they reproduce. Ocean temperatures, meanwhile, are rising within the span of only a few coral generations. A trait that spreads slowly over centuries is of little help against a change that arrives within decades.

[3] The pattern of bleaching events makes the problem worse. A reef that bleaches badly may need ten years or more to recover its living coral cover, and only if conditions allow. In the past, severe heat events on a given reef were usually separated by long intervals. Today, on many reefs, they arrive only a few years apart, so a reef is struck again before it has recovered from the last blow. Even tolerant corals cannot pass on their tolerance if they die before they spawn.

[4] I do not dismiss the experiments showing that some corals tolerate heat better than others; they are real and valuable. But a coral that survives one degree of extra warming may still fail at two. Experiments in aquariums also tend to test one stress at a time, while a real reef may face heat, pollution, and disease in the same summer. Tolerance has limits, and on many reefs those limits are already being approached.

[5] Nursery programs and local protection are worth supporting. Yet they should be described honestly: as ways to buy time, not as solutions, and they can reach only a small part of the world's reefs. The only lasting protection for reefs is to slow the warming of the oceans themselves.
questions.q: The main purpose of Passage A is to argue that:
c: bleaching is harmless to corals because they always recover.
all coral species will adapt to warmer seas without human help.
corals have natural ways of responding to heat that give reefs a real, though uncertain, chance of surviving.
nursery programs should replace efforts to reduce pollution and overfishing.
questions.e: Haddad describes several ways corals adjust but also says 'None of this means that reefs are safe.' A and B are too extreme (she says a bleached coral 'may starve'); D reverses her view, since she wants local protection AND nurseries.

Passage III — Humanities: This passage is adapted from an essay about the history of shadow-puppet theatre.

[1] Of all the ways human beings have found to tell stories, few require less equipment than the shadow play. A sheet of thin cloth, a lamp behind it, and a handful of flat figures cut from leather or card are enough. Yet from these simple materials, performers across Asia, the Middle East, and parts of Europe built one of the most lasting forms of popular theatre, one that entertained audiences for centuries before cinema projected its first flickering images onto a screen.

[2] Exactly where the shadow play began is still debated. Traditions in China, India, and Southeast Asia all claim great age, and the stories told about their beginnings tend to be legends rather than records. One Chinese tale describes a grieving emperor who was shown the shadow of a figure behind a curtain and believed, for a moment, that a lost loved one had returned. Whether or not anything like this ever happened, the legend points to something true about the art: from the beginning, audiences have been moved less by what the puppets are than by what they seem to become in the light.

[3] On the Indonesian islands of Java and Bali, the form known as wayang kulit grew into a long and serious art. A performance could last through an entire night, and a single puppet master, called the dalang, would voice every character, move dozens of finely cut and painted figures, and direct the musicians who played beside him. The stories, many of them drawn from ancient epics, were not only entertainment but also lessons in conduct, and audiences understood the battles on the screen as struggles between order and disorder, duty and desire.

[4] The Arab world developed its own shadow theatre, known in Arabic as khayal al-zill, "the imagination of the shadow." Some of the oldest shadow plays to survive in written form were composed in Cairo in the thirteenth century by Ibn Daniyal, a writer who had moved to Egypt from Mosul. His plays are crowded with comic characters from city life, such as boastful soldiers, false doctors, and swindlers, and they mix rough jokes with clever wordplay. That combination tells us something about the audience: these were performances for ordinary people, but for ordinary people who enjoyed language as much as slapstick.

[5] Under the Ottomans, the shadow play spread widely across the eastern Mediterranean, and in Turkey it came to center on two famous characters, Karagöz and Hacivat. Karagöz is blunt, impulsive, and plain-spoken; Hacivat is polite, educated, and a little pompous, fond of long words that his companion constantly misunderstands. Their quarrels could be adapted endlessly to local events. A performer might mock a greedy merchant or a new tax without naming anyone, letting the shadows say what a speaker in the street might not dare to say.

[6] That freedom was part of the form's power, but the form itself was fragile. Shadow theatre depended on live performers who knew their audiences, and on audiences who gathered in coffeehouses and courtyards during festivals and long evenings. When cinema, radio, and later television arrived in the twentieth century, they offered entertainment that was cheaper, more convenient, and available every night. In many cities, the shadow screens went dark within a generation.

[7] Still, the art has not disappeared. Wayang kulit continues to be performed in Indonesia, and both it and the Karagöz tradition have been recognized by UNESCO as part of the world's intangible cultural heritage. In Egypt and elsewhere, small troupes and puppet makers have brought the old characters back for new audiences, sometimes in schools, sometimes at festivals. They face the question that every revival faces: whether to preserve the old plays exactly, or to let the shadows speak, as they always did, about the present.

[8] Perhaps the answer lies in the form's own history. The shadow play lasted so long not because it stayed the same but because each generation of performers made it its own. A figure of painted leather has no voice until someone behind the screen gives it one.

c: began in Cairo and later spread east to Asia.
was completely destroyed by the arrival of cinema.
was mainly a religious ceremony performed by priests.
is a simple but lasting art form that survived for centuries by adapting to its audiences and times.
questions.e: The essay traces the form across regions, its decline, its revival, and ends by saying it lasted 'because each generation … made it its own.' B is too extreme: paragraph 7 says 'the art has not disappeared'; A contradicts paragraph 2, which says the origin is debated and names Asian traditions.

Passage IV — Social Science: This passage is adapted from an article about a study of young people who move from small towns to cities. The researcher, the study, and its figures are fictional.

[1] Every year, millions of young people around the world pack a bag, say goodbye to the town where they grew up, and board a bus or a train to a city. More than half of the world's population now lives in urban areas, and young adults make up a large share of those who move. Their decisions shape both the places they leave and the places they go. Yet the question of why they move is often answered too quickly. "For jobs" is the usual reply, and it is not wrong. It is, however, incomplete.

[2] To understand the decision more fully, a research team led by the sociologist Nadia Fawzy surveyed 2,400 people aged 18 to 29 who had moved from small towns and villages to large cities within the previous five years. The respondents came from many different regions, and about half of them were women. Instead of offering a single box marked "work," the survey asked each person to choose the main reason for the move from a list and then to describe, in their own words, what else had influenced the decision.

[3] The table shows the main reasons respondents chose, divided into two age groups.

Main reason for moving | Ages 18–23 | Ages 24–29
Education | 41% | 12%
Work or higher pay | 28% | 47%
Family (joining relatives or marriage) | 9% | 21%
Lifestyle and services | 17% | 14%
Other | 5% | 6%

[4] The most striking pattern is how the reasons change with age. Among the younger group, education was the leading reason: many had moved to attend a university or a training institute that did not exist near home. Among the older group, work came first by a wide margin, and family reasons more than doubled. Fawzy argues that these are not two separate kinds of migrants but, in many cases, two stages of one life. "Someone moves at nineteen to study," she writes, "and stays at twenty-five because the city is now where the jobs, the friends, and often the husband or wife are."

[5] The written answers added detail that numbers alone could not. Many respondents described the city less as a place of opportunity than as a place of choice. In a small town, one woman explained, "there is one pharmacy, one kind of job, and one opinion about how you should live." Others mentioned hospitals, fast internet, or simply the freedom of being unknown: no one in the city knew their family, and no one reported their movements back home. These lifestyle factors were the main reason for only a minority, but they appeared as a secondary influence in more than half of all the written answers.

[6] The survey also complicates a common worry about rural areas. It is often assumed that once young people leave, they cut their ties with home. Yet most respondents said that they regularly sent money or goods to relatives, and many said that they hoped to return one day, though few had a specific plan for doing so. Fawzy cautions that a hope to return is not the same as a return, but she notes that ties to home remain strong for years after a move.

[7] What does this mean for towns that want to keep their young people? Fawzy's answer is that jobs alone will not be enough. A town that gains a factory but not a college, a clinic, or reliable internet may slow the departure of twenty-five-year-olds while doing little for eighteen-year-olds who leave to study. The decision to move, her research suggests, is rarely about one thing. It is a weighing of many, and the weights change as a person grows older. Some towns, she notes, have begun to treat the question less as a matter of stopping young people from leaving and more as a matter of giving them reasons to come back.

A town that gains a factory but not a college, a clinic, or reliable internet may slow the departure of twenty-five-year-olds while doing little for eighteen-year-olds who leave to study. The decision to move, her research suggests, is rarely about one thing. It is a weighing of many, and the weights change as a person grows older. Some towns, she notes, have begun to treat the question less as a matter of stopping young people from leaving and more as a matter of giving them reasons to come back.
questions.q: In paragraph 7, the example of a town that gains a factory but not a college mainly serves to:
c: argue that factories do more harm than good to small towns.
show that a single kind of improvement may address one age group's reasons for leaving but not another's.
compare industrial towns with university towns in other countries.
suggest that older respondents care only about jobs.
questions.e: The factory might 'slow the departure of twenty-five-year-olds' (work matters most to them) while 'doing little for eighteen-year-olds who leave to study,' matching the table. D is too extreme: older respondents also gave family and lifestyle reasons.

blocks.title: After the test
items: Read **every** explanation, including the ones for questions you got right: check that you chose the answer for the right reason.

List your wrong answers by category (Key Ideas and Details, Craft and Structure, Integration of Knowledge and Ideas) and by trap (too extreme, half-right, reversed, not in the passage, wrong paragraph).

Weak on main ideas, details and inferences? Go back to **Key Ideas and Details**. Weak on purpose, word meaning and structure? Review **Craft and Structure**. Weak on paired passages, tables and evidence? Review **Integration of Knowledge and Ideas**.
If you ran out of time, re-read **ACT Reading Strategy: Read Fast, Answer Smart** and practise the 10-minute-per-passage plan.
Wait a few days, then take **ACT Reading — Practice Test 1** (if you have not yet) under the same timed conditions and compare.
